weeks.title: Breaking Barriers & Seeing Problems
weeks.summary: Week 0 marked the beginning of our ProtoSem journey. It was less about immediately building solutions and more about understanding people, ourselves, our surroundings, and the purpose of technology.
story: Across four days, we moved from being strangers within a diverse cohort to becoming a connected team. Through icebreakers, self-awareness activities, collaborative challenges, problem-identification exercises, and AI-focused sessions, we began developing the mindset required to approach real-world problems differently.

Day 1 — Starting Conversations & 360° Interaction. The first day focused on breaking initial barriers and connecting with people from different backgrounds and disciplines. We began with personal introductions and cross-disciplinary conversations, which helped us step outside our comfort zones and interact with peers we had never met before. The Rock-Paper-Scissors activity turned networking into an energetic and engaging experience. Moving across teams and interacting with different people gradually reduced our hesitation and encouraged open communication. The day then shifted from connecting with people to observing the world around us. We were introduced to the idea of identifying real societal problems based on everyday experiences rather than assuming problems from a distance. Daily Reflection: “We started by getting to know people — and then started looking at the world around us differently.” Key Takeaway: Connection + Observation = The Start of Problem-Solving.
![Day 1 — 360° Interaction & Cross-Disciplinary Networking along the campus walkway](/photos/00week/WhatsApp Image 2026-09-10 at 6.25.30 PM.jpeg)

Day 2 — Self-Awareness & Diverse Perspectives. Day 2 focused on understanding ourselves and appreciating how differently people perceive the world. Through 16 Personalities and Web Stories, we explored different personality types, cognitive patterns, and ways of thinking. This helped us recognize that people can approach the same situation from completely different perspectives. We also explored Zen Pencils, selecting stories and comics that connected with our personal, academic, or lived experiences. Presenting these stories encouraged us to look beyond the content itself and connect narratives with our own personalities, experiences, and values. The activity demonstrated how the same story can create completely different interpretations depending on the person experiencing it. Daily Reflection: “We discovered that diversity is not just about different backgrounds — it is also about different ways of thinking.” Key Takeaway: Perspective is shaped by how we uniquely interpret the world.
![Day 2 — Exploring self-awareness, Zen Pencils, and diverse perspectives during cohort sessions](/photos/00week/WhatsApp Image 2026-09-10 at 6.25.31 PM (1).jpeg)

Day 3 — Team Formation, Collaboration & Rapid Prototyping. Day 3 was about transforming a group of individuals into a functioning team. Our Beta Team was formed, and an Among Us-inspired icebreaker helped break the remaining tension within the group. We then participated in observation challenges that encouraged active listening, discussion, and collaborative thinking. The Marshmallow Tower Challenge pushed us to work under constraints using simple materials such as spaghetti sticks, tape, thread, and marshmallows. Rather than focusing only on the final tower, the challenge taught us about communication, experimentation, iteration, and adapting when an idea does not work. Through these activities, we began understanding each other's strengths and working styles. Daily Reflection: “We stopped being just people in the same team and started becoming a team that could work together.” Key Takeaway: Shared Challenges + Active Listening = Trust & Alignment.
![Day 3 — Marshmallow tower prototyping, team collaboration, and celebration](/photos/00week/WhatsApp Image 2026-09-10 at 6.25.31 PM.jpeg)

Day 4 — Intentional Technology & Future Vision. Day 4 introduced us to the broader vision of technology, artificial intelligence, and purposeful problem-solving. The ProtoSem Inauguration Ceremony at SKT, KCT provided valuable insights from the distinguished guest speaker and helped us understand the larger purpose behind the program. During the TECH Talk on Prompt Engineering and AI Tools, we explored prompt engineering, personalized AI workflows, and how different AI tools can be selected according to specific needs and problem statements. One of the most important lessons was that technology should not be used simply because it is available. Its value comes from using the right technology for the right purpose and within the right domain context. Daily Reflection: “We learned that technology becomes more powerful when we know how to use it intentionally.” Key Takeaway: Purpose-Driven AI + Domain Context = Impactful Solutions.
![Day 4 — ProtoSem Inauguration Ceremony and cohort gathering at the SKT campus terrace](/photos/00week/WhatsApp Image 2026-09-10 at 6.25.29 PM.jpeg)

Week 0 represented a clear evolution in the way we interacted and worked together: Strangers → Self-Awareness → Teamwork → New Perspectives → Connected Team. What began with simple introductions gradually developed into collaboration, shared understanding, and a stronger sense of purpose.

What We Took Away: 01 — Connection. We learned to interact with people beyond our comfort zones and build meaningful connections across disciplines. 02 — Problem Discovery. We began training ourselves to observe everyday situations and recognize real societal problems worth solving. 03 — Self-Awareness. We gained a better understanding of different personalities, cognitive styles, and the influence of individual perspectives. 04 — Collaboration. We experienced how different ideas, strengths, and approaches can come together to achieve a shared goal. 05 — AI Awareness. We learned that AI and technology become truly valuable when they are applied intentionally to specific problems and contexts.

Final Reflection: “ProtoSem didn't just teach us new concepts. It taught us how different people can connect, think differently, and create together.” Week 0 laid the foundation for everything that followed. Before learning how to build solutions, we first learned how to connect, observe, understand, collaborate, and think with purpose.
weeks.lesson: ProtoSem didn't just teach us new concepts. It taught us how different people can connect, think differently, and create together.

weeks.title: Understanding Ideas, Design & Business
weeks.summary: Week 1 built on the foundation established during Week 0 by moving from observation and collaboration toward structured thinking, design, technology, and business understanding.
story: Throughout the week, we explored how technology influences decisions, how design thinking helps solve problems, how businesses create value, and how different industries approach real-world challenges. The week also gave us opportunities to connect classroom concepts with practical business contexts through activities, guest lectures, and presentations.

Day 1 — Recommendation Algorithms & Design Thinking. The week began with a Tech Talk on Recommendation Algorithms, introducing us to how technology can influence the content, products, or choices presented to users. We also explored Design Thinking with Meera, focusing on approaching problems from a user-centered perspective rather than immediately jumping to solutions. The day's activity applied these ideas to an eyewear retail scenario, allowing us to think about a real-world business problem through a design-oriented lens. Key Takeaway: Understand the user and the problem before designing the solution.
![Day 1 — Vedhika presenting on Instagram recommendation algorithms and content sorting logic](/photos/01week/WhatsApp Image 2026-09-10 at 5.59.35 PM (1).jpeg)

Day 2 — Data, Design & Business Analysis. Day 2 focused on the relationship between data, design, and business decision-making. The Tech Talk introduced us to Power BI dashboards and how data can be transformed into meaningful visual insights that support better decisions. We also explored IDEO and its approach to Design Thinking, gaining another perspective on how structured design methodologies can be applied to real-world problems. The day's activity focused on Value Chain and SWOT Analysis, helping us look at a business from multiple angles — from how value is created to understanding its strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats. Key Takeaway: Good decisions come from combining data, structured thinking, and an understanding of the business.
![Day 2 — Interactive session on data-driven business frameworks and the 80:20 Pareto Principle](/photos/01week/WhatsApp Image 2026-09-10 at 6.00.06 PM.jpeg)

Day 3 — Onam. Day 3 was a break from the regular technical and analytical sessions as we celebrated Onam together. The celebration provided an opportunity to connect with the cohort beyond classroom activities and experience the cultural side of campus life. Key Takeaway: Learning and collaboration also grow through shared experiences outside the classroom.

Day 4 — Prospect Theory & Building Our Portfolio. Day 4 introduced us to Prospect Theory, exploring how people make decisions when faced with gains, losses, and uncertainty. The concept encouraged us to think about decision-making not simply as a rational process, but as something influenced by how people perceive outcomes. We also worked on our portfolios, beginning to document our learning journey, experiences, skills, and progress throughout ProtoSem. Key Takeaway: Understanding how people think and make decisions is important when designing meaningful solutions.

Day 5 — Technology, Motivation & Industry Perspectives. The final day brought together technology, motivation, and real-world industry perspectives. The Tech Talk on Base 44 introduced us to another technological concept/tool as part of our continuing exploration of emerging technology. We also had a Motivation session with Ram, which provided perspective on personal growth, learning, and maintaining the mindset needed throughout the ProtoSem journey. A guest lecture on Agriculture, Textile, and Retail businesses expanded our understanding of how different industries operate and the kinds of challenges they face. The week concluded with our Week 1 Presentation, giving us an opportunity to reflect on the week's learning and communicate our understanding to the cohort. Key Takeaway: Technology becomes more meaningful when we understand the people, businesses, and industries in which it is applied.
![Day 5 — Cohort discussions and final week presentation inside the Forge studio](/photos/01week/WhatsApp Image 2026-09-10 at 6.00.06 PM (1).jpeg)
Week 1 expanded our perspective beyond simply identifying problems. We began learning how to analyze problems through different lenses — technology, design, data, business, and human behavior.
The progression of the week can be viewed as: Technology → Design Thinking → Data → Business Analysis → Human Behavior → Industry Context.

What We Took Away: 01 — Technology Awareness. We explored concepts such as recommendation algorithms, Power BI, Prospect Theory, and Base 44, expanding our understanding of how technology can influence real-world applications. 02 — Design Thinking. Through Design Thinking sessions and activities, we learned the importance of understanding users and approaching problems systematically. 03 — Data-Driven Thinking. Power BI introduced us to the importance of presenting data clearly so that information can support meaningful decisions. 04 — Business Understanding. Value Chain and SWOT Analysis helped us examine how businesses create value and respond to their internal and external environments. 05 — Human-Centered Thinking. Prospect Theory encouraged us to consider how human behavior and perception influence decision-making. 06 — Industry Exposure. The guest lecture covering agriculture, textile, and retail gave us a broader view of how concepts we learn can connect to different industries. 07 — Reflection & Communication. Creating our portfolio and presenting our Week 1 learning helped us document, organize, and communicate our experiences.

Final Reflection: “Week 1 taught us to look at problems from more than one angle — understanding the user, the technology, the data, the business, and the industry before thinking about a solution.” Week 1 helped us move from simply observing problems to understanding the different perspectives and frameworks that can be used to analyze them.
weeks.lesson: Week 1 taught us to look at problems from more than one angle — understanding the user, the technology, the data, the business, and the industry before thinking about a solution.

weeks.title: From Problems to Programs
weeks.summary: Week 2 marked a shift from understanding problems and design approaches toward structured problem-solving and computational thinking.
story: The week introduced us to the fundamentals of defining a problem, representing solutions logically, and gradually transforming ideas into working programs using visual programming tools.

Day 1 — Problem Statements & 5S. The week began with problem statements and the 5S approach. We learned the importance of clearly defining a problem before attempting to solve it. Rather than immediately thinking about a solution, the focus was on understanding and structuring the problem properly. Key Takeaway: A clearly defined problem is the first step toward a meaningful solution.

Day 2 — Algorithms & Flowcharts. Day 2 introduced algorithms and flowcharts. We learned how to break a problem into a sequence of logical steps and represent those steps visually through flowcharts. This helped bridge the gap between identifying a problem and actually designing a systematic solution. Key Takeaway: Think logically, break the problem into steps, and represent the solution clearly.

Day 3 — Introduction to Scratch. Day 3 introduced us to Scratch, providing a visual and interactive way to understand programming concepts. Through block-based programming, we began translating logical ideas into executable instructions without having to focus heavily on programming syntax. Key Takeaway: Programming begins with logic and problem-solving, not just writing code.

Day 4 — MIT. Day 4 introduced MIT, continuing our exploration of programming and technology through practical learning. The session helped connect the concepts of problem-solving, algorithms, and visual programming with a broader technology-oriented learning environment. Key Takeaway: Turning an idea into a working solution requires both logical thinking and the right tools.
Week 2 helped us understand the journey from identifying a problem to representing and implementing a solution.
The learning progression was: Problem Statement → Algorithm → Flowchart → Scratch → MIT.

What We Took Away: 01 — Problem Definition. Learned to understand and clearly frame a problem before developing a solution. 02 — Logical Thinking. Used algorithms to break problems into manageable, sequential steps. 03 — Visual Representation. Used flowcharts to communicate and understand the logic of a solution. 04 — Programming Fundamentals. Explored Scratch as an accessible way to convert logical thinking into programs. 05 — Technology & Application. Continued connecting problem-solving concepts with practical technology tools.

Final Reflection: “Week 2 taught us that solving a problem is not about jumping directly to a solution. It is about understanding the problem, thinking logically, planning the steps, and then turning that plan into something that works.”
weeks.lesson: Week 2 taught us that solving a problem is not about jumping directly to a solution. It is about understanding the problem, thinking logically, planning the steps, and then turning that plan into something that works.

weeks.title: OS Setup, Linux Deployment & Practical Electronics
weeks.summary: From OS installation and Linux terminal game development to Vercel deployment and practical electronics with breadboards and circuits.
story: Day 1 — Operating System Installation & System Setup. Learned the fundamentals of system setup and operating system installation. Linga guided us through the process of booting a system, preparing installation media, and installing an operating system. We also gained an understanding of the basic steps involved in configuring a system after installation.

Day 2 — Linux Terminal Game Development & Deployment. Explored the Linux environment and learned how to work with the Linux terminal. We developed a game that runs through the terminal, gaining practical experience with Linux commands, file management, and running projects in a Linux environment. We also started deploying the game using Vercel.
![Day 2 & 3 — Studio presentation and project discussion on Linux terminal game deployment](/photos/03week/WhatsApp Image 2026-09-29 at 9.55.00 PM.jpeg)

Day 3 — Vercel Deployment & Portfolio–Obsidian Integration. Continued working on the deployment of our Linux game through Vercel and learned more about hosting and deploying web-based projects. We also explored connecting our portfolio with Obsidian to create an activity-based workflow, with the goal of automatically updating weekly posts and activities on the portfolio.

Day 4 — Fundamentals of Electronics. Started learning the fundamentals of electronics under the guidance of Brahma. We were introduced to basic electronic components and their practical applications. The session included hands-on work with breadboards, LEDs, and basic electronic circuits.
![Day 4 — Hands-on testing of capacitor voltage limits and power supply characteristics](/photos/03week/WhatsApp Image 2026-09-29 at 9.52.56 PM.jpeg)
![Day 4 — Cohort collaborating around the electronics lab bench during component testing](/photos/03week/WhatsApp Image 2026-09-29 at 9.52.55 PM (1).jpeg)

Day 5 — Practical Electronics & Circuit Building. Continued our practical electronics sessions by working with breadboards, LEDs, and other basic electronic components. We learned how to identify components, understand their connections, and build simple circuits while developing a foundation in basic electronics and hardware interfacing.
![Day 5 — Perfboard circuit prototyping with LED indicator, resistor, and tactile switch](/photos/03week/WhatsApp Image 2026-09-29 at 9.52.55 PM.jpeg)
weeks.lesson: Week 3 bridged systems and physical computing — from configuring operating systems and deploying terminal applications to building our first practical electronic circuits.

weeks.title: Arduino, Sensors & ESP32 Development
weeks.summary: Hands-on exploration of Arduino, sensor interfacing with IR and DHT11, and building interactive games and autonomous traffic signals with ESP32.
story: Day 1 — Introduction to Arduino & Basic Control. We were introduced to Arduino, its components, programming environment, and basic hardware interfacing. We started with simple hands-on experiments, including controlling an LED and adjusting its brightness level using Arduino. This helped us understand digital and analog control and how software can interact with electronic components.
![Day 1 — Embedded Systems lecture & microcontroller architecture briefing on studio display](/photos/04week/WhatsApp Image 2026-09-29 at 9.55.58 PM.jpeg)

Day 2 — Arduino & Sensor Interfacing. We explored how sensors can be integrated with Arduino to collect and process real-world data. We worked with sensors such as the IR sensor and DHT11 temperature and humidity sensor. We learned how to read sensor values, process the data through Arduino, and display the results. We also documented our experiments and prepared technical reports based on the sensor implementations.
![Day 2 — Arduino Uno microcontroller interfacing with DHT11 temperature and humidity sensor module](/photos/04week/WhatsApp Image 2026-09-29 at 9.55.58 PM (1).jpeg)

Day 3 — Introduction to ESP32 & Interactive Game Development. We were introduced to the ESP32 and its capabilities for wireless and hardware-based applications. We experimented with LEDs, joysticks, and other components connected through breadboards. Using the ESP32 and joystick inputs, we developed an interactive game where the game interface was displayed on a screen and controlled through physical joystick inputs.
![Day 3 — Hands-on firmware development and game logic coding in Arduino IDE](/photos/04week/WhatsApp Image 2026-09-29 at 9.55.58 PM (2).jpeg)

Day 4 — ESP32 & Autonomous Traffic Signal. We continued working with ESP32 and explored the integration of multiple sensors and output components. We developed an autonomous traffic signal system using two IR sensors, red and green LEDs, and an ESP32. The system used sensor input to detect traffic conditions and control the corresponding signal automatically, giving us practical experience in sensor-based automation.
![Day 4 — Autonomous traffic signal prototype wired with dual IR sensors and LED indicators on ESP32](/photos/04week/WhatsApp Image 2026-09-29 at 9.55.59 PM (1).jpeg)

Day 5 — ESP32-Based Maze Game & Hardware Integration. We further explored ESP32-based interactive applications by developing a maze game controlled using joysticks. The game was displayed on a laptop while the physical joystick inputs were connected through the ESP32 and breadboard. This project helped us understand the integration of hardware inputs, microcontrollers, wireless communication, and software-based game interfaces.
![Day 5 — Assembling joystick breadboard circuitry and hardware testing at the workbench](/photos/04week/WhatsApp Image 2026-09-29 at 9.55.59 PM.jpeg)
weeks.lesson: An embedded system bridges logic and reality — software gives the hardware a mind, and sensors give it senses.

weeks.title: UI/UX Design & Problem Validation
weeks.summary: From problem identification, user research surveys, and validation to crafting user-centered UI/UX prototypes and flows in Figma.
story: Day 1 — Problem Identification & Team Formation. We were introduced to the fundamentals of UI/UX and the importance of understanding user needs before developing a solution. We learned about basic UI principles, including the importance of color selection, color palettes, visual consistency, and user-friendly interface design. We then formed teams and began identifying real-world problems that could be addressed through technology.

Day 2 — Problem Statement Validation & User Research. We focused on validating our selected problem statement to ensure that it addressed a genuine user need. We conducted surveys and collected responses from different users to understand their experiences, requirements, and challenges. The collected feedback helped us evaluate and refine our problem statement.

Day 3 — Research Analysis & Figma UI/UX Design. We analyzed the information gathered through our surveys and converted our findings into a structured solution concept. We were introduced to Figma and began designing the UI/UX of our proposed solution. We focused on creating a clear, consistent, and user-friendly interface while applying the UI/UX principles we had learned.

Day 4 — Solution Development & UI/UX Refinement. We continued developing our solution based on the validated problem statement and refined the Figma designs. We worked on improving the overall user flow, interface structure, visual elements, and usability of the proposed system.

Day 5 — Solution Submission & Presentation. We finalized our problem statement, research findings, and UI/UX design. The completed solution concept and Figma prototype were submitted as the outcome of the week's work, marking the transition from problem identification and research toward solution development.
weeks.lesson: A meaningful solution starts with listening — validating real user needs through research and clear UI/UX design before building the final product.

weeks.title: Laser Cutting, 3D Printing & Digital Fabrication
weeks.summary: Comprehensive technical guide and laboratory documentation on laser cutting processes, 3D printing technologies, thermoplastic filaments, and H2S machine specifications.
story: # Laser Cutting
## What is Laser Cutting?

Laser cutting is a digital manufacturing process that uses a concentrated laser beam to cut, engrave, or mark materials according to a digital design. The laser produces intense heat that melts, burns, vaporizes, or removes the material along the programmed path. It is commonly used with materials such as acrylic, wood, cardboard, MDF, leather, and certain plastics.
## Laser Cutting Process
**Design Creation** — A 2D design is created using CAD or vector-design software.
**File Preparation** — The design is converted into a compatible format such as DXF, SVG, AI, or PDF, depending on the machine and software.
**Machine Parameter Setup** — Appropriate power, speed, frequency/PPI, and cutting or engraving settings are selected.
![CAD vector path simulation and parameter setup in laser cutting software for Loki silhouette](/photos/06week/new/WhatsApp Image 2026-09-28 at 12.37.07 PM (1).jpeg)
**Material Placement** — The material is positioned correctly on the laser cutting bed.
**Laser Focusing** — The laser head is adjusted to the correct focal distance for the selected material.
**Testing** — A small test cut or engraving is performed to verify the selected parameters.
![Operating the industrial laser cutting machine at FabLab Forge](/photos/06week/WhatsApp Image 2026-09-30 at 9.14.54 AM.jpeg)
**Cutting or Engraving** — The machine follows the digital design and uses the laser to cut or engrave the material.
![Laser cutting process in action on the honeycomb bed](/photos/06week/WhatsApp Video 2026-09-29 at 10.53.46 PM (2).mp4)
**Finishing** — The finished pieces are removed from the machine and cleaned or finished if required.
![Precision laser cutting & engraving on black acrylic](/photos/06week/WhatsApp Image 2026-09-29 at 10.53.52 PM.jpeg)
## Advantages of Laser Cutting

* High precision and accuracy
* Produces complex shapes easily
* Fast for many 2D fabrication tasks
* Minimal physical contact with the material
* Suitable for both cutting and engraving
* Digital designs can be easily modified
* Good repeatability
* Produces detailed cuts and engravings
## Disadvantages & Considerations

* Initial machine cost can be high
* Requires proper ventilation and safety precautions
* Some materials can produce harmful fumes
* Heat can cause burning or discoloration
* Not every material is suitable for laser cutting
* Thick materials may require multiple passes
* Requires correct power and speed settings
## Types of Laser Cutting
**CO₂ Laser Cutting** — Uses a carbon-dioxide laser and is widely used for non-metal materials such as wood, acrylic, MDF, paper, and plastics.
**Fiber Laser Cutting** — Uses a fiber-based laser source and is mainly used for cutting and marking metals such as steel, stainless steel, aluminum, and brass.
**Nd:YAG / Nd:YVO₄ Laser Cutting** — Uses solid-state laser technology and is commonly used for specialized industrial cutting, marking, and precision applications.
**Diode Laser Cutting** — Uses semiconductor laser diodes and is generally used for lower-power applications such as engraving and cutting thinner materials.
# 3D Printing
## What is 3D Printing?

3D printing is an additive manufacturing process in which a physical three-dimensional object is created by building material layer by layer from a digital 3D model. Unlike traditional manufacturing, which often removes material from a larger block, 3D printing adds material only where it is required.
## 3D Printing Process
**3D Model Creation** — A model is designed using software such as Fusion 360 or obtained from an online 3D model repository.
**Model Export** — The model is exported in a suitable format, commonly STL or 3MF.
**Slicing** — Slicing software converts the 3D model into individual layers and generates machine instructions, commonly in the form of G-code.
![3D CAD model on the slicer build plate ready for layer generation](/photos/06week/new/WhatsApp Image 2026-09-30 at 9.24.20 AM.jpeg)
**Print Configuration** — Settings such as layer height, infill, temperature, print speed, and support structures are configured.
**Filament Loading** — The required printing material is loaded into the printer.
**Bed Preparation** — The print bed is cleaned and leveled or calibrated.
**Printing** — The printer deposits or cures the material layer by layer to create the physical object.
![Bambu Lab 3D printer depositing filament layer by layer](/photos/06week/WhatsApp Video 2026-09-29 at 10.54.45 PM.mp4)
**Post-Processing** — Supports are removed and the finished object may be cleaned, sanded, or otherwise processed.
## Advantages of 3D Printing

* Can produce complex geometries
* Useful for rapid prototyping
* Reduces material waste in many applications
* Allows easy design modifications
* Supports customization and personalization
* Useful for prototypes and educational projects
* Can produce functional parts
* Suitable for small-batch production
## Disadvantages & Considerations

* Printing can be slow for large objects
* Surface quality may require post-processing
* Mechanical properties can vary depending on print orientation
* Some materials require controlled printing conditions
* Support structures may be required
* Large industrial printers can be expensive
* Dimensional accuracy depends on the printer and print settings
## Types of 3D Printing
**FDM / FFF (Fused Deposition Modeling)** — A heated nozzle melts thermoplastic filament and deposits it layer by layer. Common materials include PLA, ABS, PETG, TPU, and Nylon.
**SLA (Stereolithography)** — Uses a light source to selectively cure liquid photopolymer resin layer by layer. It provides high detail and smooth surfaces.
**MSLA / LCD Resin Printing** — Uses a UV light source and an LCD masking system to cure an entire layer of resin at once.
**SLS (Selective Laser Sintering)** — Uses a laser to selectively fuse powdered material layer by layer. Nylon and other polymer powders are commonly used.
**SLM / DMLS (Metal 3D Printing)** — Uses a high-energy laser to fuse or melt metal powder. These technologies are commonly used for industrial metal components.
# 3D Printing Filaments
A filament is the raw thermoplastic material used by many FDM/FFF 3D printers. Filaments are commonly available in diameters such as 1.75 mm and 2.85 mm / 3.00 mm, depending on the printer.
## Common Filament Types
**PLA (Polylactic Acid)** — Easy to print, relatively low warping, and commonly used for prototypes, models, and decorative objects.
**ABS (Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene)** — Durable and more temperature-resistant than PLA. Commonly used for functional parts and enclosures.
**PETG (Polyethylene Terephthalate Glycol)** — Provides good strength and durability while being relatively easy to print. Often used for functional components.
**TPU (Thermoplastic Polyurethane)** — A flexible, rubber-like filament used for grips, flexible components, and protective parts.
**Nylon** — Strong, tough, and wear-resistant. Often used for engineering and mechanical applications.
**ASA (Acrylonitrile Styrene Acrylate)** — Offers good UV and weather resistance, making it suitable for outdoor applications.
**PC (Polycarbonate)** — A strong, heat-resistant material used for demanding engineering applications.
## Important Filament Properties

* Nozzle temperature & bed temperature
* Printing speed & layer height
* Tensile strength & impact resistance
* Flexibility & rigidity balance
* Thermal resistance & heat deflection
* Moisture sensitivity & storage
* Warping tendency
* Environmental & UV resistance
# H2S 3D Printer
If the H2S machine refers to the 3D printer available at the Forge laboratory, the exact specifications should be verified from the machine's model number or specification sheet.
![Configuring 3D print job on the touchscreen panel with AMS unit](/photos/06week/WhatsApp Image 2026-09-30 at 9.14.41 AM.jpeg)

## Basic Working of the H2S Printer
3D Model → STL / 3MF → Slicing → G-code → Filament Loading → Bed Preparation → Layer-by-Layer Printing → Support Removal → Finished Object
weeks.lesson: Digital fabrication bridges software design and physical reality — mastering machine parameters, material constraints, and fabrication tolerances turns digital models into durable physical products.

weeks.title: Give the idea a system
weeks.summary: Connecting inputs, logic, outputs, and the edges between them.
story: The selected concept is broken into functional parts: sensing, processing, feedback, and power. A block diagram documents the interfaces between these parts and highlights where failure could propagate.

Candidate components are compared using their actual constraints, including voltage requirements, communication protocols, and physical size. The highest-risk integration is prioritized for an early bench test.
weeks.lesson: The space between components deserves as much attention as the components themselves.

weeks.title: Meet the hardware
weeks.summary: The first circuit, the first reading, and the first practical surprises.
story: Assembly starts with a minimal circuit and verified power rails. One component is introduced at a time, with basic checks recorded before the system grows more complicated.

A sensor reading becomes the first end-to-end signal. Unstable results are treated as evidence to investigate rather than something to smooth away immediately. Connections, sampling intervals, and environmental conditions are checked in turn.
weeks.lesson: A smaller working system is easier to understand than a larger mysterious one.

weeks.title: Teach it to respond
weeks.summary: Moving from raw signals to predictable, meaningful behavior.
story: The sample firmware separates input collection, decision logic, and output updates. Explicit states make startup, normal operation, and sensor failure observable instead of implicit.

Test inputs are used to check transitions without relying on unpredictable real-world conditions. Clear fallback behavior is designed for disconnected components and invalid readings so the prototype does not imply confidence it does not have.
weeks.lesson: Good behavior includes what happens when the expected input never arrives.

weeks.title: Give it a physical form
weeks.summary: CAD, material constraints, and an enclosure that serves the interaction.
story: The enclosure is modeled around the actual components and their interfaces. Openings, fastening points, and access for assembly are considered before visual refinement.

A first print is used to check fit rather than prove that the design is finished. Tolerances, sensor exposure, cable paths, and the visibility of feedback all become practical inputs to the next revision.
weeks.lesson: A beautiful enclosure still has to open, fit, connect, and be understood.

weeks.title: Bring the pieces together
weeks.summary: The first complete prototype, and everything integration reveals.
story: Hardware, firmware, and the physical enclosure are brought together for a full task walkthrough. The focus is not simply whether each part works, but whether the experience remains coherent when they work together.

Issues are logged with reproduction steps, expected behavior, and observed behavior. A short integration checklist makes each revision easier to evaluate and prevents a fixed problem from quietly returning.
weeks.lesson: Integration is its own design activity, not the last step after design.

weeks.title: Let someone else try
weeks.summary: Stepping back and watching the prototype meet fresh eyes.
story: Test sessions give participants a realistic task without explaining the intended interaction first. The facilitator watches for hesitation, repeated actions, and interpretations that differ from the design assumptions.
Feedback is separated into observed behavior, participant comments, and proposed solutions. This keeps the team from implementing every suggestion without understanding the underlying difficulty.
weeks.lesson: If you have to explain the interface, you have learned something about the interface.

weeks.title: Change what matters
weeks.summary: Prioritizing useful fixes over a growing wish list of features.
story: The observed issues are ranked by their effect on the core task. Ambiguous status feedback and unclear recovery paths take priority over cosmetic inconsistencies.

A focused revision changes only a small set of related behaviors. The previous test tasks are repeated so that a promising improvement is checked against the same criteria rather than judged from memory.
weeks.lesson: Iteration is most useful when you can explain what changed and why.

weeks.title: Make the signal clear
weeks.summary: A calmer digital interface with feedback people can understand.
story: A companion interface explores how to display current conditions and recent changes without implying false precision. Clear labels explain the meaning and freshness of each reading.
Color is supported by text and shape so it is not the only source of information. Loading, empty, and disconnected states are designed with the same care as the normal dashboard.
weeks.lesson: Useful information includes enough context to interpret it correctly.

weeks.title: Test the edges
weeks.summary: Power cycles, missing signals, and all the less convenient realities.
story: The prototype is tested through deliberate interruptions: power cycling, sensor disconnection, and invalid input. Each case records whether the system detects the issue and how it communicates recovery.

Limitations are documented rather than hidden. A simple test matrix distinguishes repeatable behavior from observations that still require longer-term validation, keeping the claims proportionate to the evidence.
weeks.lesson: Reliability begins with an honest understanding of the boundaries.

weeks.title: Build a repeatable demo
weeks.summary: Turning a promising prototype into a clear, dependable demonstration.
story: The demonstration is organized around one understandable scenario. A setup checklist, known initial state, and fallback plan reduce the chance that incidental setup problems obscure the work.
The narrative introduces the user need before the technology. Each demonstrated feature is connected to a specific problem so the audience can evaluate its purpose, not just its technical novelty.
weeks.lesson: A good demo makes the value visible before it makes the technology impressive.

weeks.title: Tell the whole story
weeks.summary: Documenting not just what was made, but why it became that way.
story: Research notes, sketches, test observations, and revisions are assembled into a case study. The structure follows the decisions that shaped the work rather than presenting a frictionless sequence of successes.
Images receive useful captions, evidence is distinguished from interpretation, and unfinished questions remain visible. The documentation aims to help someone understand and continue the project.
weeks.lesson: The decisions behind the artifact are part of the artifact's value.

weeks.title: Share, listen, refine
weeks.summary: A final review that creates better questions for what comes next.
story: A practice presentation invites critique of both the prototype and the claims made about it. Reviewers are encouraged to identify unclear reasoning, unsupported conclusions, and practical gaps.

The final revisions prioritize clarity and accuracy. The team prepares direct answers about what was tested, what remains a concept, and what further evidence would be needed before real-world deployment.
weeks.lesson: Credible work is comfortable explaining its limitations.

weeks.title: An ending. A beginning.
weeks.summary: Looking back at the making, and forward to the next worthwhile question.
story: The final sample week brings the prototype, process documentation, and learning journal together. The outcome is evaluated against the original brief, with the project's evolution made explicit.

A reflection identifies the habits worth carrying forward: asking better questions, making smaller tests, preserving evidence, and listening without defending. The next steps are deliberately modest and grounded in what the journey actually revealed.
weeks.lesson: The most lasting outcome is a better way to approach the next unknown.

blogs.title: Technical // From Prompts to Prototypes
blogs.excerpt: I went into ProtoSem expecting the technical track to start with a tool. Instead, it started with a warning: don't use technology just because it's available.

sections.heading: Lesson One: A Tool Is Only as Useful as the Problem It's Matched To
sections.body: The Week 0 Tech Talk on prompt engineering wasn't really about clever prompt tricks. It was about intentionality — picking the right AI tool for a specific need, inside a specific domain, instead of throwing the newest tool at every problem. That idea kept resurfacing across later sessions, from recommendation algorithms to Power BI to Base44, where each concept was tied to a real decision it could help someone make.

sections.heading: Lesson Two: Before Code, There's Logic
sections.body: Week 2 is where 'intentional technology' became practical. Before we touched an app-building platform, we spent a full day on algorithms and flowcharts. That exercise reframed what programming means: not syntax first, but breaking a messy task into a sequence clear enough for a machine or another person to follow without guessing. Flowcharts made that logic visible before a single line of code existed.

sections.heading: Lesson Three: Play First, Precision Later
sections.body: Scratch came right after the algorithms session, and the contrast was almost funny. After structured flowcharts, we were suddenly building memes and interactive projects in a drag-and-block interface. That low-stakes environment removed the fear of syntax errors and let us focus on whether the underlying logic of our project actually made sense.

sections.heading: Lesson Four: Real Constraints Change Everything
sections.body: The real technical shift happened on Day 4 of Week 2, with MIT App Inventor. Suddenly the algorithms and flowchart thinking had a real job to do: mapping out how a real app should behave, not just how a hypothetical process should flow. Working with block-based programming kept the emphasis on structure and logic, but because the problem behind it was real, the stakes felt different.

sections.heading: The Technical Thread So Far
sections.body: Looking back, the technical arc of these three weeks hasn't been about accumulating tools. It's been: intentional tool selection → visible logic → low-stakes experimentation → real application. Each week added one more layer of rigor onto the last, but the throughline never changed — understand the problem and the logic before reaching for the tool.

blogs.title: Reflections // Bridging People & Perspectives
blogs.excerpt: Three weeks into ProtoSem, I've started noticing that the 'soft' parts of this program were never really soft. They were the foundation everything technical eventually stood on.

sections.heading: Strangers, By Design
sections.body: Week 0 didn't ease us into anything. It threw us straight into a room of people we'd never met and asked us to talk, play, and observe together before we'd even learned each other's names properly. The Rock-Paper-Scissors activity made the first conversation happen before the awkwardness had time to set in. Later, 16 Personalities and Zen Pencils showed how differently two people can read the same story, and the Marshmallow Tower Challenge turned that insight into a real team test.

sections.heading: The In-Between Moments Matter More Than You Think
sections.body: By Week 1, the cohort didn't feel like strangers anymore, but the bonding didn't stop — it just moved into different spaces. Onam wasn't on the technical syllabus, but it let people be people outside of problem statements and frameworks. I noticed conversations during Onam went deeper than most structured team discussions, simply because nobody was trying to solve anything.

sections.heading: Collaboration Gets Harder (and More Honest) Once There's Something to Build
sections.body: Week 2 is where I really saw the difference our first two weeks had made. When we sat down with Scratch, the goal was low-stakes — build something funny, experiment, make memes. But watching how naturally the team split up ideas, tried each other's suggestions without ego, and laughed through failed attempts told me something important: the trust from Week 0 had not disappeared. It had simply been waiting for a real task to show up.

sections.heading: What I'm Taking From This
sections.body: If I'm honest, none of the technical content so far required a huge leap for me. What actually shifted was subtler: I've started noticing perspective as a variable, not a given. ProtoSem hasn't just been teaching us how to build something. It's been quietly teaching us how to build with people — which, three weeks in, feels like the harder and more useful skill of the two.

blogs.title: Innovation // Prototyping Under Constraint
blogs.excerpt: If there's one myth ProtoSem has quietly dismantled for me, it's that innovation starts with a good idea. Three weeks in, I'd argue it actually starts with a good constraint.

sections.heading: Constraint #1: A Handful of Spaghetti Sticks
sections.body: The earliest version of this lesson showed up in Week 0's Marshmallow Tower Challenge — spaghetti, tape, thread, and one marshmallow, all structured into a race against the clock. The instinct was to plan the perfect tower first and build it once. That instinct failed almost immediately. What actually worked was the opposite: build something rough, watch it fall, notice why, adjust, and rebuild. The lesson wasn't really about towers. It was that constraints don't kill creativity; they force it to move faster and get honest sooner.

sections.heading: Constraint #2: A User You Don't Actually Know Yet
sections.body: Week 1 introduced a subtler constraint — not a resource limit, but a knowledge limit. In the Design Thinking session applied to an eyewear retail scenario, the challenge wasn't coming up with ideas. It was resisting the urge to design for an imagined customer instead of understanding what an actual customer might need. The same discipline showed up again in Value Chain and SWOT Analysis, where the goal was to map where value was created before proposing a solution.

sections.heading: Constraint #3: A Problem That Has to Earn Its Place
sections.body: Week 2 is where 'constraint' became literal project scope. We spent nearly half a day just choosing a problem statement, and that turned out to be one of the most useful parts of the week. It's tempting to pick the first inconvenience that comes to mind, but the 5S approach and the later problem validation step reminded us that not every problem deserves your time, and figuring out which ones do is its own skill.

sections.heading: What Constraint Actually Buys You
sections.body: Across all three weeks, the pattern repeats: fewer resources, fewer assumptions, or fewer allowed problem statements didn't slow innovation down — it sharpened it. The spaghetti tower forced fast iteration. The design thinking sessions forced real user empathy instead of assumption. The problem validation process forced us to earn the right to start building. None of this matches the popular image of innovation as a lightning-bolt idea. It's slower, more deliberate, and a little uncomfortable — but that discomfort is where clearer thinking begins.
